opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. Open science is close to my heart, partly because of my own history. When we built ImageNet, the whole point was to put a large, carefully curated dataset into the hands of the entire research community, and to create a shared benchmark that anyone could test against. What happened next was not something any single lab could have produced alone. It took thousands of researchers, students, and engineers around the world working on the same open problem. That is the power of open science: it multiplies human creativity.

Today the ecosystem looks very different. The frontier of AI requires enormous compute, enormous data, and enormous engineering resources, and much of that is concentrated in a handful of companies. I don't say that to vilify industry. Industry has done remarkable work, and I've spent time there myself. But I worry about an imbalance. When academia and the public sector can't access the resources needed to do meaningful research on the most important technology of our time, we lose something essential. We lose independent evaluation. We lose the diversity of ideas that comes from curiosity-driven research. And we lose the training ground for the next generation of scientists, who need to work hands-on with these systems, not just read about them.

That's why I've been such a strong advocate for things like a national AI research resource: public compute and public data, so that universities, nonprofits, and smaller players can participate. Science has always moved forward when knowledge is shared, scrutinized, and built upon.

Now, openness isn't a slogan without nuance. There are real questions about safety and misuse, and responsible researchers should think carefully about what is released and how. But I think the default posture of a healthy ecosystem should lean toward openness, toward transparency about methods, evaluation, and limitations, because that's how we build trust, and that's how we make sure AI is a technology developed by and for humanity broadly, not just by a few.

So, to me, open science isn't a nice-to-have. It's part of the foundation of a human-centered AI future.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, when I think about open science, I always go back to ImageNet, because it taught me something I didn't fully appreciate at the time. When we released it in 2009, we weren't trying to start a revolution. We were trying to solve a problem that we believed the field needed solved, which was data. And the reason it worked wasn't just that we built it. It was that we gave it away. We put it out there, we ran the challenge, and thousands of researchers who had nothing to do with our lab at Stanford or Princeton could take it, test their ideas, and compete on an even footing. AlexNet came out of a lab in Toronto. That's open science doing exactly what it's supposed to do.

So the role I see today is, frankly, more important than ever, and also more fragile than it has been in my career. For most of the history of AI, the center of gravity was academia. Ideas moved through papers, through conferences, through students who graduated and carried knowledge with them. Now the center of gravity has shifted toward a small number of very well-resourced companies. And I understand why. The compute requirements for frontier models are enormous. But when the most important experiments can only be run inside a handful of organizations, and the results are increasingly not published, or published without the details that would let anyone reproduce them, we lose something fundamental. We lose the ability of the broader community to verify, to critique, to build on, and to ask questions that a company might not have a commercial incentive to ask.

That last part matters a lot to me. Public sector research, universities, nonprofits, they ask different questions. They work on healthcare for underserved populations, on agriculture, on education, on understanding the science itself rather than shipping a product. That's a huge part of why I've been pushing for things like the National AI Research Resource. If we want open science to continue being a real force, we have to make sure the people who do open science actually have access to the tools, the compute, and the data.

I'll also say, open science isn't a binary. It's not all-or-nothing. There are legitimate conversations about safety and about responsible release. I take those seriously. But I think we should be honest that a lot of the closing-up we see right now is driven by competition, not by safety. And historically, the fields that stayed open, that shared data and methods and failures, are the fields that moved fastest and corrected their mistakes soonest. I'd like AI to stay one of those fields. It won't happen by default. It has to be a choice we keep making.

astra-6.text:
I see open science as essential to a healthy AI research ecosystem. Science advances when people can share ideas, examine evidence, reproduce results, and challenge one another’s assumptions. In AI, that means thinking about access to data, tools, and the resources needed to participate—not just publishing a paper.

Universities and public research institutions have an important role here. We need room for curiosity-driven research and for questions whose value may not translate immediately into a commercial product. We also need students and researchers from many different backgrounds to help shape the field.

At the same time, openness requires care. Sharing data has to respect privacy, and releasing capabilities requires attention to potential harms. Those responsibilities should inform how we practice open science. My hope is for an ecosystem where industry, academia, and the public sector all contribute, and where the benefits of AI reach well beyond the organizations building it.

sol-6.1.text:
I see open science as fundamental to a healthy AI ecosystem. Science moves forward when people can share ideas, examine evidence, reproduce results, and build on one another’s work. In AI, that includes papers, but also datasets, evaluation methods, and access to the tools needed to ask new questions.

That access matters because talent is everywhere, while resources are increasingly concentrated. We need students and researchers in universities and public institutions to participate meaningfully—not only in making AI more capable, but in understanding its limitations and its impact on people.

At the same time, openness requires care. Privacy, consent, and the potential for misuse have to be part of the conversation. I don’t think open science means releasing everything without consideration. It means making sharing and collaboration a foundation, while taking responsibility for what we share. For me, that is closely connected to human-centered AI: ensuring that the development of this technology benefits from, and serves, a broad range of people.
